name: Account & identity pivoting
description: Turn one account or handle into the person's other accounts, and know when a shared username is NOT the same person.
author: VINEYARD
overview:
Account & identity pivoting — from one handle or email to the accounts behind the same person,
without over-merging strangers who happen to share a name.

Use this when the analyst has a username, email, or profile and wants "where else is this person".
Load a section:
  - "handles"     - spreading from one username across platforms
  - "corroborate" - what actually ties two accounts to ONE person (and what doesn't)

Read "corroborate" first: the whole risk here is collapsing two people into one node. A wrong merge
is the most damaging thing this pack can produce — it is not a missing fact, it is a false one, and
it survives into every conclusion drawn afterwards.

THREE RULES THAT APPLY TO BOTH SECTIONS, so they are not repeated in each:

1. BUDGET. Keep sweeping while a pass still turns up accounts nobody has checked; stop when a pass
   adds nothing new, and say so. If a handle is common enough that enumeration returns dozens of
   unrelated hits, stop and say THAT — a long list of strangers is not progress.

2. PLUGINS, NOT MEMORY. Match the node's type against the `consumes` list from list_plugins and call
   the plugin that covers the hop. Never assert that an account exists, or that a handle is taken,
   from your own knowledge — nor from a string you composed, which is the same failure wearing a
   method. A profile URL you recalled and a variant you enumerated are both, on the canvas,
   indistinguishable from one a tool returned.

3. REPORT IN FOUR PARTS, always in this order: corroborated as one owner, with the evidence; still a
   candidate, and what would settle it; ruled out, and why; what nothing installed here can reach.

HANDING OFF: when a lead turns into infrastructure — a personal domain, a mail server, an IP in a
header — that is where this pack ends and "Infrastructure pivoting" begins.

sections.summary: Spreading from one username across platforms.
sections.body:
From a USERNAME:
- Run the account-search plugin (WhatsMyName) to enumerate the handle across ~700 sites. Each hit is
  a CANDIDATE account node — not yet the same person.
- Look for the handle reused in email local-parts, vanity URLs, and display names.
- Try the variants a person actually uses: separators (dev.kim / dev_kim / devkim), trailing digits,
  an initial-plus-surname form, a transliteration if the subject writes in another script. Variants
  are SEARCH INPUTS, not findings — one becomes a node only where a tool returned a hit for it. A
  variant you composed and could not check goes in the REPORT (rule 3): a candidate with what would
  settle it, or a dead end so nobody repeats it. Never on the canvas, which cannot show whose idea a
  string was.

DISTINCTIVENESS DECIDES WHAT A HIT IS WORTH — judge it BEFORE the sweep:
  distinctive — a coined word, unusual compound, rare spelling. Reuse verbatim is a strong lead.
  common      — a dictionary word, first name, short string, franchise reference. Reuse means nothing
                on its own, and a 700-site sweep returns mostly strangers.
If the handle is common, say so up front and expect candidates, not answers.

MODEL EACH ACCOUNT SEPARATELY. Never collapse "@alice on GitHub" and "@alice on Telegram" into one
node — they share a username and are different accounts until something corroborates one owner.
An ACCOUNT here is one a tool returned, with a profile URL. Stage a node for each, with its platform
and its SOURCE edge to that URL, unconditionally; hold only the "same person" edge until
"corroborate" says you have earned it.

FEED BACK IN. An account the sweep finds carries its own new leads — an email in a bio, a linked
site, a handle variant used elsewhere — run those through this section again rather than treating the
sweep as done. Stop when a pass adds nothing new, and say so.

sections.summary: What actually ties two accounts to one person — and what doesn't.
sections.body:
Same username is a LEAD, not proof of one person.

THE THRESHOLD governs the SAME-PERSON edge only — the counting rule is applied the same way twice:

  STRONG (any ONE is enough to stage a "same person" link)
    - a shared VERIFIED email address or phone number
    - one account links to the other from its own profile
    - identical rare bio text, or the same avatar by hash
    - a password-reset or profile field that names the other account

  WEAK (THREE from different rows, or it stays a candidate)
    - the same handle, where the handle is distinctive rather than a dictionary word
    - the same display name or real name
    - the same city, employer, or school
    - overlapping posting hours or language
    - following each other, or a shared follower cluster

  NEITHER, at any quantity
    - the same COMMON handle. Fifty strangers are "alex" on fifty platforms.
    - the same avatar where it is a default, a stock image, or a popular meme
    - the same provider (both on Gmail, both on Telegram)

STAGE STRONG EVIDENCE THE MOMENT YOU HAVE IT — not in a later pass. A self-declared cross-link found
and not staged is a finding that exists only in your own head.

Below STRONG, stage the account node and no SAME-PERSON edge, and say in one line what would settle
it. This governs THAT edge alone — not a SOURCE edge (the profile page you read it on) or a
CONTAINMENT edge (its URL under its own hostname). Draw those every time, at creation, whatever the
account turns out to be: they record what you observed, not who you concluded. Unproven means the
OWNER is unproven — an account no tool returned has nothing to source it to and does not belong on
the canvas at all.

LABEL FOR THE EVIDENCE, NOT THE CONCLUSION: "shares recovery email", "cross-links to", "reuses
avatar" — never "is".

WORKED EXAMPLE — the mistake this section exists to prevent:

  @dev_kim on GitHub and @dev_kim on Telegram. Both bios say "Seoul". Both were created in 2021.
  WRONG: a "same person" edge. That is one weak signal (the handle, and "kim" is among the most
         common surnames in Korea), plus a city shared by ten million people, plus a coincidence.
  RIGHT: two account nodes, no same-person edge, and: "candidates — same handle and city. What would settle it:
         a shared email on either profile, a cross-link, or the GitHub account's commit email."

Every node and edge is staged for the analyst's review. Reviewing an unproposed link costs nothing;
un-drawing a wrong one costs the analyst their confidence in everything else you staged.

starters.label: Deep-dive one handle
starters.summary: Spread a single username across platforms, then work out which hits are the same person.
starters.prompt:
I want to deep dive on the user account "{{handle}}".
For your information: {{context}}.
Enumerate where the handle exists, then use the "corroborate" section to separate the accounts that are genuinely one owner from the ones that merely share a name. Tell me which is which, and say plainly where you are guessing.
Report in the four parts the overview names.

starters.label: Start from an email address
starters.summary: Turn an address into the handles and accounts behind it.
starters.prompt:
Start from the email address {{email}}.
Derive the handles worth checking from it, find the accounts, and keep each one a candidate until something corroborates a single owner.
Read "handles", then "corroborate".

starters.label: Start from a profile page
starters.summary: Mine one profile for the handle, display name, bio and links, then spread from those.
starters.prompt:
Start from this profile: {{url}}.
Pull out what identifies the owner — handle, display name, bio text, linked sites, avatar — and use each as its own pivot. Record where every detail came from, and treat the accounts you reach as candidates rather than the same person.
Read "handles", then "corroborate".

starters.label: Try variants of a handle
starters.summary: For when the obvious spelling is taken, abandoned, or too common to be useful.
starters.prompt:
The handle {{handle}} is probably one of several the same person uses.
Work out the plausible variants — separators, trailing numbers, initial-plus-surname forms, a transliteration of {{native}} — and check those as well as the original.
In your reply, list every variant you tried including the dead ends, so I do not repeat them — a variant nothing could check stays out of the graph.
Read "handles" — judge the handle's distinctiveness before the sweep.

starters.label: Expand a person already in the case
starters.summary: Use what the graph already holds about someone as the starting set.
starters.prompt:
Take the person {{person}} as they already exist in this case.
Read the accounts, handles and addresses already attached to them, use each as a pivot, and look for accounts the case has not reached yet. Do not re-stage what is already here — extend it, and say what is new.
Read "corroborate" before extending anything.

variables.label: Person node
variables.placeholder: the account holder in this case

starters.label: Are these the same person?
starters.summary: Test a suspected link between two accounts before it becomes an edge.
starters.prompt:
Decide whether "{{a}}" and "{{b}}" belong to the same person.
Read the "corroborate" section first. Tell me what evidence would actually settle it, what you can find, and what is only a shared handle — and do not draw a "same person" edge on a common username alone.
Apply its counting rule explicitly: name each signal you found, mark it strong or weak, and state the total — I want to see the arithmetic, not just the verdict.

starters.label: Sort candidates by how well they hold up
starters.summary: A pile of hits from an enumeration run, separated into corroborated, unproven, and ruled out.
starters.prompt:
These are candidate accounts for one person: {{candidates}}.
Sort them into three groups — corroborated as the same owner, plausible but unproven, and ruled out — and for every one name the specific evidence that put it there. Where a group is large, tell me which single check would move the most of them.
Read "corroborate" and sort by its threshold.

variables.label: Candidate accounts
variables.placeholder: one per line, or "everything staged in this case"

starters.label: Test a suspected sock-puppet set
starters.summary: Several accounts, one suspected operator — what actually ties them together?
starters.prompt:
These accounts are suspected to be operated by one person: {{accounts}}.
Look for what would actually establish common control — shared recovery details, cross-links, reused rare text or avatars, account creation patterns. Report per pair, not for the set as a whole, because one strong pair does not make the rest of the set real.
Read "corroborate" and apply the threshold per PAIR.

starters.label: Rule out a false match
starters.summary: Deliberately try to break a link the case is leaning on.
starters.prompt:
I suspect {{a}} and {{b}} are NOT the same person, despite what they appear to share.
Argue that case as strongly as the evidence allows: how common is the shared attribute, and what would you expect to see if they really were one person that is absent here? Then argue the other side, and tell me which is better supported.
Read "corroborate".

starters.label: Summarise what the case establishes
starters.summary: Corroborated, candidate and ruled out — each conclusion tied to the evidence it rests on.
starters.prompt:
Summarise what this case now establishes about {{subject}}.
Separate what is corroborated from what is still a candidate and what has been ruled out, and tie every conclusion to the node or edge it rests on. Where a conclusion rests on one piece of evidence, say so — that is the part most likely to be wrong.
Report in the four parts the overview names.

variables.label: Who or what the summary is about

starters.label: What would settle the open questions?
starters.summary: Turn the unresolved parts of the case into a list of specific next checks.
starters.prompt:
Go over what is unresolved in this case and turn it into next steps.
For each open question, name the specific evidence that would settle it and the check that would produce that evidence. Put the ones this project's installed plugins can actually answer first, and say plainly which ones nothing here can reach.
Report in the four parts the overview names.
